questions.questionText: The stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower consisting of:
questions.explanation: The stamen consists of the anther (produces pollen grains containing male gametes) and the filament (stalk supporting the anther).

questions.questionText: Pollination is the:

options.text: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma

questions.diagram: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma, which is a prerequisite for fertilisation in plants.

questions.questionText: Self-pollination occurs when pollen lands on:

options.text: A different flower on the same plant

questions.explanation: Self-pollination occurs when pollen from an anther lands on the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.

questions.questionText: Wind-pollinated flowers are characterised by:

options.text: Large, feathery stigmas and lack of petals

questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers (e.g., grasses, maize) have small, inconspicuous flowers with large feathery stigmas to catch pollen, and tasselled stamens producing abundant lightweight pollen.

questions.questionText: Asexual reproduction in plants that involves roots, stems, or leaves is called:
questions.explanation: Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction using plant parts (runners, tubers, bulbs, cuttings) to produce genetically identical offspring.

questions.questionText: Insect-pollinated flowers typically have:
questions.explanation: Insect-pollinated flowers attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators with bright colours, nectar, and fragrances.

questions.questionText: The ovule develops into the:
questions.explanation: After double fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed containing an embryo (from the zygote), endosperm (food store), and seed coat (from integuments).

questions.questionText: The part of the flower that develops into the fruit is the:
questions.explanation: Following fertilisation, the ovary wall develops into the fruit, which protects the seeds and aids in their dispersal.

questions.questionText: Cross-pollination leads to greater genetic diversity because it involves:
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination combines genetic material from two different parent plants, producing offspring with novel combinations of traits.

questions.questionText: Vegetative propagation by runners (stolons) is seen in:
questions.explanation: Strawberry plants produce stolons (runners) that grow horizontally above ground, producing new plantlets at nodes that can grow independently.

questions.questionText: The pollen tube grows through the:
questions.explanation: After landing on the stigma, the pollen grain germinates and the pollen tube grows down through the style to deliver sperm cells to the ovule in the ovary.

questions.questionText: Double fertilisation in angiosperms results in:

options.text: One embryo and one seed coat

questions.diagram: Double fertilisation produces two structures: a diploid zygote (forms embryo) and a triploid endosperm (forms food storage tissue).

questions.questionText: A complete flower has:
The advantage of asexual reproduction in plants is:
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction enables rapid multiplication without flowers, pollinators, or seeds, which is advantageous when pollinators are scarce or environmental conditions are stable.

questions.questionText: Which plant structure is a modified underground stem that stores food?
questions.explanation: A tuber is a swollen underground stem that stores starch. The potato is a stem tuber (from stolons) with buds (eyes) that can sprout into new plants.

questions.questionText: Apomixis refers to:

options.text: Asexual reproduction through seeds without fertilisation

questions.explanation: Apomixis is asexual seed production where an embryo develops without gamete fusion, producing offspring genetically identical to the parent.

questions.questionText: Endosperm in angiosperm seeds is important because it:

options.text: Provides nutrition for the developing embryo

questions.diagram: Endosperm is a triploid food storage tissue that provides nutrients (starch, oils, proteins) for the developing embryo during germination.

questions.questionText: Which mechanism of seed dispersal relies on the fruit becoming sticky or hooked?
questions.diagram: Fruits with sticky surfaces or hooks (e.g., burdock) attach to animal fur or feathers, dispersing seeds to new locations as animals move.

questions.questionText: The synergids and antipodal cells in the embryo sac:

options.text: Degenerate after fertilisation (synergids) or have no function (antipodals)

questions.diagram: Synergids guide pollen tube entry and typically degenerate after fertilisation. Antipodal cells may support the embryo sac but have limited known function.

questions.questionText: Grafting in horticulture involves:

options.text: Joining the vascular cambium of a scion and rootstock so they grow as one plant
Inserting a cutting directly into soil to root

questions.explanation: Grafting joins the cambium layers of a scion (desired variety) and rootstock (root system) so vascular tissues fuse and the scion grows as the new plant.
